**Answer: Yes.** For all sufficiently large $k$, the set $\{b_1 f_k, b_2 f_k, \dots, b_n f_k\}$ is linearly independent.

---

**Proof.**

Let $V = \operatorname{span}\{b_1, \dots, b_n\} \subset B$. Since $\{b_i\}_{i=1}^n$ is linearly independent, $V$ is $n$-dimensional. Define linear functionals $\psi_i : V \to \mathbb{C}$ ($i = 1, \dots, n$) by
$$\psi_i(b_j) = \delta_{ij}.$$
These are continuous (every linear functional on a finite-dimensional normed space is continuous). By the Hahn–Banach theorem, each $\psi_i$ extends to a bounded linear functional $\varphi_i \in B^*$ on all of $B$, still satisfying
$$\varphi_i(b_j) = \delta_{ij}, \qquad 1 \le i, j \le n. \tag{1}$$

Since $\{f_k\}$ is an approximate unit of the C*-algebra $B$, it is a two-sided contractive approximate unit, so for every $a \in B$,
$$\|a f_k - a\| \to 0 \quad \text{as } k \to \infty. \tag{2}$$

For each $k$, form the $n \times n$ matrix
$$M_k[i,j] := \varphi_i(b_j f_k), \qquad 1 \le i, j \le n.$$

Because each $\varphi_i$ is bounded (hence continuous) and $b_j f_k \to b_j$ in norm by (2),
$$M_k[i,j] = \varphi_i(b_j f_k) \xrightarrow{k \to \infty} \varphi_i(b_j) = \delta_{ij} \quad \text{by (1)}.$$

Thus $M_k \to I_n$ entrywise, and since $\det$ is a polynomial (hence continuous) in the matrix entries,
$$\det M_k \to \det I_n = 1 \neq 0.$$

Consequently there exists $K$ such that for all $k \ge K$, $\det M_k \neq 0$, i.e. $M_k$ is invertible.

**Claim.** For every $k \ge K$, the set $\{b_1 f_k, \dots, b_n f_k\}$ is linearly independent.

Indeed, suppose $\sum_{j=1}^n \lambda_j\, b_j f_k = 0$ for some scalars $\lambda_j \in \mathbb{C}$. Applying $\varphi_i$ to both sides gives
$$\sum_{j=1}^n \varphi_i(b_j f_k)\,\lambda_j = \sum_{j=1}^n M_k[i,j]\,\lambda_j = 0, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n.$$
This is the homogeneous linear system $M_k \lambda = 0$. Since $M_k$ is invertible, $\lambda = 0$. Hence $\{b_1 f_k, \dots, b_n f_k\}$ is linearly independent. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
